title: Make chlorine from salt water with a pool salt cell
summary: A salvaged pool salt cell run on low-voltage DC in a bucket of brine makes a weak sodium hypochlorite solution, a home-made bleach for disinfecting drinking water once salt is all you have left. It gives off hydrogen, which can explode, and chlorine gas, so run it outdoors away from flames; and never use the solution until a pool test kit has told you how strong it is.

materials.item: Pool or spa salt chlorinator cell (the electrolytic cell from the return pipe), with its DC cable
DC supply you can limit: a bench supply with an adjustable current limit, or batteries (two 12 V in series make 24 V). Not the pool's own control box
Fuse and holder, rated a little above the current you plan to run, for the positive lead
Multimeter able to read amps in series, or a clamp ammeter for DC
Open plastic tub or bucket, 15–20 L, left uncovered while it runs
Plain salt, at least 99 % sodium chloride: no iodine, no anti-caking agent, not rock salt
Pool or spa test kit that reads free chlorine (DPD)
Opaque plastic bottle with a cap, labelled, for the solution
1 mL and 5 mL syringes and a measuring jug

steps.text: Know what you are making: a weak sodium hypochlorite solution, the same chemical as household bleach. Purpose-built units make about 5 g/L (0.5 %) from salt water at 25 g/L (SSWM WATA). Use found bleach or pool chlorine while you have it; this is for when you don't. You also need a pool test kit that reads free chlorine: without one, don't use the solution on drinking water. Boiling needs no kit.
Set up outdoors, in the open and in moving air (not under a roof or overhang), well away from flames, stoves, smokers, sparks and any doorway or air intake.
steps.warn: The cell makes hydrogen at the negative plates and chlorine at the positive ones (RSC brine). Hydrogen burns in air at anything from 4 to 75 % (Xylem hydrogen); chlorine is toxic (RSC brine). Never run it indoors, in a shed or in a closed container.

steps.text: Inspect the cell. If the plates are crusted with white scale, flush it off with a hose or scrape with plastic or wood, never metal, which strips the plate coating (Hayward AquaRite S3).

For stubborn scale only, outdoors and with gloves and goggles on (Jandy AquaPure): soak the cell in 4 parts water to 1 part muriatic acid for a few minutes, acid added to water, cable end kept dry, then rinse it well (Hayward AquaRite S3).
steps.warn: Rinse every trace of acid off before the cell goes back in brine or near bleach: acid and hypochlorite together give off chlorine gas. See [Shop chemicals](#ref/reference_chemicals/never_mix).

steps.text: Mix the brine in the open tub: 25 g of salt per litre of clean water, so 375 g in 15 L (SSWM WATA). Use only plain salt that is at least 99 % sodium chloride, with no iodine and no anti-caking agent, and not rock salt (Hayward AquaRite S3, Jandy AquaPure). Use clear water, and let any cloudy brine settle before pouring off the clear part (SSWM WATA).
Stand the cell upright in the brine with its top end open to the air, so gas bubbles straight out and away. Keep the cable connections above the liquid.
steps.warn: Never run a cell inside a closed pipe, capped bottle or sealed tub: Jandy warns that a cell with no flow builds up flammable gas (Jandy AquaPure).

steps.text: Wire it to DC only, with a meter in series and a fuse in the positive lead close to the battery or supply ([Wiring 12 V and 24 V DC systems](#guides/skill_dc_wiring)). Pool control boxes feed their cells low-voltage DC: Jandy's give 22–30 V at up to 3 A, or 6 A for the larger model (Jandy AquaPure). The makers' ratings are for their own controllers and pool plumbing, so this limit is a cautious choice, not a rating: stay at or below what the cell's own controller gave it, and start at a low voltage.
steps.warn: Don't use the pool control box with its flow switch bypassed. Put any mains-fed supply on a GFCI outlet, dry (Jandy AquaPure). Switch off before touching any wire: a spark at a loose clip near the bubbles can light the hydrogen (Xylem hydrogen). Keep batteries away from the bucket.

steps.text: With the supply off, make every connection and check that the plates are under brine and the cable ends are dry. Switch on and watch the meter for the first minute. If the current is above your limit, switch off, then use a weaker brine or a lower voltage before trying again.

Run it for a fixed time, note the amps and minutes, then switch off, unplug, and wait for the bubbling to stop before lifting the cell out. Switch off early if you smell a sharp, bleachy swimming-pool smell (RSC brine). That smell warns of chlorine only: hydrogen has no smell (DOE hydrogen). Start with a short run and lengthen it only after you have tested a batch; this guide has no tested run time for this setup. Write down what you did, so a batch you tested can be repeated.

Test the strength before any of it goes near drinking water: put a measured 1 mL into 10 L of clean, chlorine-free water and read free chlorine with the pool kit, as in [Test how strong old bleach is](#guides/test_bleach_strength). With 1 mL in 10 L, the reading in mg/L is the strength in percent. A weak solution such as WATA's 0.5 % reads only about 0.5 mg/L that way, so use 5 mL in 10 L if the kit shows nothing or sits at its lowest mark: the strength in percent is then the reading divided by 5. Never put the neat solution in the kit: above about 10 mg/L the reagent bleaches out and reads falsely low (Taylor FAQ).

Pour it into a clean, labelled, opaque bottle and stand it outdoors, away from sun and flame, with the cap loose while it settles: hydrogen keeps coming out of fresh solution (Xylem hydrogen). Then cap it, keep it cool and out of children's reach, and use it within 24 hours (SSWM WATA). Make a fresh batch rather than keep an old one, and never pour new solution into a bottle that holds old (WHO chlorate).

Dose clear water by the tested strength. WATA's guide for its 0.5 % solution is 5 mL per 20 L (SSWM WATA), which is 25 mg of chlorine in 20 L. For a different strength, keep to 25 mg per 20 L: mL per 20 L = 2.5 ÷ strength in percent (0.25 % needs 10 mL, 1 % needs 2.5 mL). Double the dose for cloudy water or water colder than 10 °C (HealthLinkBC disinfecting). Clearing the water first is better than doubling.

Wait at least 30 minutes, and 1 to 2 hours if the water is colder than 10 °C (HealthLinkBC disinfecting), then test: free chlorine should read at least 0.5 mg/L if the pH is below 8 (WEDC Mobile Note 7, quoting WHO); at pH 8 or above, see [Test water with found kits](#guides/test_water). More only tastes stronger: WHO's health-based value for free chlorine is 5 mg/L (WHO chlorine value). Too low, dose again and wait; nothing at all, the solution is too weak or the water is dirty.
steps.warn: Chlorine is weak against Cryptosporidium (WHO chlorine test). For water from ponds, rivers or anything with animals near it, filter first or boil instead.

steps.text: Rinse the cell, tub and syringes in clean water when you finish, and drain and store the cell where it can't freeze: ice damages it (Hayward AquaRite S3). Pour leftover solution out on bare ground well away from wells and streams (this guide's own precaution; none of its sources covers disposal).

notes:
## What it is
A salt cell is a stack of coated metal plates in a short length of pipe that pool water flows through. Fed low-voltage DC, it turns the salt in the water into chlorine, which kills bacteria and algae and turns back into salt (Jandy AquaPure, Hayward AquaRite S3). The same chemistry works in a tub of brine: the result is a weak sodium hypochlorite solution, which is what household bleach is. Purpose-made devices for communities and health centres do much the same from salt, water and electricity: Antenna's WATA units make about 5 g/L (0.5 %) solution from 25 g/L brine (SSWM WATA), and MSR's SE200 runs off mains or a 12 V car battery and makes enough in a 5-minute cycle to treat up to 200 L of water (PATH SE200).

A pool cell isn't designed for this. Both makers' manuals cover the cell only in the pool's own plumbing, run by their own controllers (Jandy AquaPure, Hayward AquaRite S3). Jandy recommends 3.0 to 3.5 g/L of salt and warns that above 4.0 g/L its control box may be damaged (Jandy AquaPure); Hayward's control works from 1,200 to 8,000 ppm, which is 1.2 to 8 g/L (Hayward AquaRite S3). WATA's 25 g/L brine is about three times the top of Hayward's range. A saltier bath lets more current through at the same voltage, and in a bucket there is no flow switch and no controller holding the current down. None of the sources here says how much a pool cell draws or makes in brine that strong, so the meter and the strength test are all you have. That's why this guide is marked for experienced builders.

## The gases
- **Hydrogen** forms at the negative plates. It barely dissolves, so it bubbles out and collects at the top of anything closed. It burns in air at about 4–75 % by volume (Xylem hydrogen; a US Department of Energy fact sheet gives 4–74 %), and industrial on-site generators dilute it to 1 % in air and send it to the outdoors or a well-ventilated space (Xylem hydrogen). It has no colour or smell and rises fast, so it becomes a fire hazard mainly where something, such as a roof or a poorly ventilated room, holds it in (DOE hydrogen); that is why the open air matters, and why nothing that sparks goes near the bubbles. Xylem notes that electrodes can arc, and an arc is an ignition source (Xylem hydrogen). Jandy warns that running a cell with no water flow builds up flammable gas and is hazardous (Jandy AquaPure). Even after the run, hydrogen stays in the solution as bubbles and dissolved gas and comes out later, which is why industrial storage tanks are force-ventilated (Xylem hydrogen).
- **Chlorine** forms at the positive plates (RSC brine). In a pool cell it goes on to make the hypochlorite you want (Jandy AquaPure), but some can escape as gas, and it is toxic (RSC brine, WHO chlorine test). Breathing chlorine fumes must be avoided (WHO chlorine test).
- **Caustic:** the brine around the negative plates turns into sodium hydroxide solution, which is corrosive (RSC brine). Goggles and gloves for all of it.

So: outdoors, open tub, top of the cell open, no flame or spark within reach of the bubbles, and step back while it runs. A classroom guide to the same reaction says to switch off as soon as you smell a bleachy, swimming-pool smell (RSC brine); do the same, and let it clear. That smell warns of chlorine only: hydrogen has no smell (DOE hydrogen). In freezing weather the place for it is still the open air, not a shed to keep it warm, and the cell must never freeze with brine in it (Hayward AquaRite S3). See the [chemical hazard](#browse/hazards/chemical).

## Power and current
Pool control boxes turn mains into low-voltage DC for the cell: Jandy's smaller AquaPure gives 22–30 V DC at up to 3 A and is rated for 283 g of chlorine a day in a pool; the larger gives up to 6 A and 567 g a day (Jandy AquaPure). That's about 12 g an hour from the small one, while WATA's dose for clear water works out to about 1.25 mg per litre (5 mL of a 5 g/L solution in 20 L) (SSWM WATA). Those are a pool's ratings, not measurements for a bucket, but they show that a short run can make plenty for a household. Gas and heat rise with the current, so run short batches at a modest current.
- The original control box runs on mains and only lets the cell run when its flow sensor sees water moving (Jandy AquaPure). Don't defeat the flow switch to make it work in a bucket. Jandy also warns that above 4.0 g/L of salt its control box may be damaged, and says to connect it only to a GFCI-protected circuit (Jandy AquaPure). Leave the box out of this build, and put any mains-fed supply on a GFCI outlet, kept dry.
- A DC bench supply with a current limit, or batteries with a fuse in the positive lead and a meter in series, is the simpler route (see [Wiring 12 V and 24 V DC systems](#guides/skill_dc_wiring)). A battery has no current limit of its own: brine this strong decides how much it draws, so watch the meter from the first second. The makers' ratings are for their own controllers and pool plumbing, so this limit is a cautious choice, not a rating: stay at or below what the original controller supplied (3 or 6 A for Jandy's, Jandy AquaPure). The cell was fed 22–30 V (Jandy AquaPure), so one 12 V battery may run it only weakly; two in series give 24 V. If the current is too high, use a weaker brine or a lower voltage, not a bigger fuse. Keep any battery away from the bucket: a lead-acid battery gives off hydrogen too ([Lead-acid batteries](#guides/safety_lead_acid)).
- Controllers clean the plates by themselves (Jandy's every 3 hours) (Jandy AquaPure). In a bucket nothing does, so look for white scale between runs and clean it as in the steps.

## The salt and the water
Use plain sodium chloride that is at least 99 % pure: Hayward asks for more than 99.0 % and Jandy for at least 99.8 %, with Jandy preferring evaporated, granulated, food-quality, non-iodised salt. Both say to avoid anti-caking agents and rock salt, and Hayward also rules out iodised salt (Jandy AquaPure, Hayward AquaRite S3). Check the label: the only ingredient should be salt. Their reasons are about the cell and pool fittings, so no source here says what an additive does to water you will drink; the safe course is to use none. Make the brine with clear water: WATA's factsheet says only clear water can be used and that very cloudy water interferes with the electrolysis (SSWM WATA).

## Testing and dosing
The one hard rule: **don't treat drinking water with it until you have measured its strength.** A batch's strength is likely to depend on the salt, current, time, temperature and the cell's age, none of which you can judge by eye. [Test how strong old bleach is](#guides/test_bleach_strength) gives the method and the arithmetic: a measured amount in clean water, read with a DPD pool kit.

Then treat water at WATA's rate, scaled to your strength: clear it first, give 25 mg of chlorine per 20 L (mL per 20 L = 2.5 ÷ your strength in percent), double that for cloudy or cold water (HealthLinkBC disinfecting), wait at least 30 minutes (WHO says longer below 18 °C; HealthLinkBC says 1 to 2 hours below 10 °C), and check that at least 0.5 mg/L of free chlorine is left, at pH below 8 (WEDC Mobile Note 7, quoting WHO). More than that is not dangerous, only stronger-tasting: WHO's health-based value for free chlorine is 5 mg/L (WHO chlorine value). WATA's own advice for its 0.5 % solution is 5 mL per 20 L of water, drinkable after 30 minutes (SSWM WATA). Chlorine doesn't stop Cryptosporidium and won't remove chemicals (WHO chlorine test).

## Keeping it
Home-made hypochlorite is weak and unstabilised. WATA says to use it within 24 hours, keep it from sunlight, which breaks chlorine down, and keep it away from children (SSWM WATA). Make small batches often, and never pour new solution into a bottle that still holds old (WHO chlorate).

## Chlorate
Hypochlorite makes chlorate as it ages, and nothing in a household kit takes it out afterwards. None of the sources here measures what a pool cell in a bucket makes, and you can't test for it at home, so treat it as an open risk. What the health bodies say is about stored hypochlorite: chlorate forms as the solution sits, warm or in the light, and faster when new solution is added to old (WHO chlorate, HC chlorate). Health Canada knows of no residential-scale treatment that removes it (HC chlorate). Its limit for chlorate in drinking water is 1 mg/L (HC chlorate) and WHO's provisional value is 0.7 mg/L, with a warning that struggling to meet it must never be a reason to skip disinfecting (WHO chlorate). So use each batch fresh and within 24 hours, never keep or top up a bottle, don't dose more than the test says you need, and where you have the fuel to boil clear water, boiling avoids the question.

## Never
- never in a closed vessel, a basement, a garage or a tent;
- never near a flame, stove, smoker or anything that sparks;
- never mixed with acid, ammonia or other cleaners: see [Shop chemicals](#ref/reference_chemicals/never_mix);
- never capped tight straight after a run, or topped up into a bottle of old solution;
- never into drinking water untested.
